sections.h2: Where is Hinds County and how is it laid out?
sections.html:
Hinds County sits in central Mississippi and is the state's most populous county, with 227,742 residents at the 2020 census. It covers 877 square miles, of which 870 are land, and it has two county seats: Jackson and Raymond.

That two-seat arrangement shapes almost every property tax errand. The county is split into a First Judicial District (Jackson) and a Second Judicial District (Raymond), and the tax collector, tax assessor and chancery clerk each keep an office in both places.

The cities are Byram, Clinton, Jackson and Raymond. The towns are Bolton, Edwards, Learned, Terry and Utica, and unincorporated places such as Brownsville, Cayuga, Cynthia, Midway, Oakley and Pocahontas fill in the rural parts. Part of Jackson lies in Madison and Rankin counties, so check which county bills a given parcel.

Interstates 20, 55 and 220 cross the county, along with US 49, US 51 and US 80, and a stretch of the Natchez Trace Parkway runs through it. Public-use airports are Hawkins Field in Jackson and John Bell Williams Airport in Raymond.

sections.h2: Which Hinds County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
Three elected offices share the work: the tax assessor values property, the tax collector sends bills and takes payment, and the chancery clerk records deeds, runs the appeal hearing process through the Board of Supervisors, and collects delinquent taxes. Each has a Jackson and a Raymond location, open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday through Friday except legal holidays.

You can read each office's page on the county site: Tax Collector, Tax Assessor and Chancery Clerk.

sections.h2: How does the Hinds County assessor value a house?
sections.html:
The assessor lists every taxable parcel, estimates its value, applies the state assessment ratio and certifies a roll to the Board of Supervisors. The office says its territory runs from Learned, with about 100 parcels, up to the City of Jackson, with more than 70,000, and totals over 106,000 parcels.

Under the state's classes, a single-family, owner-occupied home is Class I and is assessed at 10 percent of true value. Other real estate, such as a rental house, is Class II at 15 percent. The Mississippi Department of Revenue explains that taxes equal true value times the assessment ratio times the millage rate.

Hinds County says it reviews 25 percent of taxable property each year, so every parcel is looked at at least once every four years. For most houses that means a drive-by comparison against the drawings and field sheet in the office. The assessor only contacts an owner if what the appraiser sees differs from the file. The state adds that interior inspections of homes are not required.

The office also runs sales ratio studies, comparing appraised values with actual sale prices, and the State Tax Commission does its own.

  • Ownership is set as of January 1 using deeds filed with the chancery clerk.
  • The assessment roll goes to the Board of Supervisors on the first Monday in July.
  • The office's past policy has been to notify owners when a new appraisal rises $2,000 or more over the prior year.

sections.h2: What dates matter on a Hinds County tax bill?
sections.html:
Taxes are due on or before February 1 for property assessed the previous year, and if February 1 falls on a weekend or legal holiday, payment is accepted the next Monday without penalty. The chancery clerk's office says statements are mailed from the tax collector each December and that current taxes may be paid in three installments.

After February 1, state law adds interest of one-half of one percent per month, or fraction of a month, on unpaid tax. The governor can extend that date by proclamation for unusual conditions, for up to 60 days at a time.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Hinds County assessment?
sections.html:
You ask the county Board of Supervisors for a hearing, and the Chancery Clerk is the contact for that request. The state says an appeal normally has to be filed by the first Monday in August before the tax comes due.

Start earlier, though. The Hinds assessor says its office will review values with an owner at any time of year, and its page describes the formal appeal as the next step under Mississippi Code 27-35-89. For business personal property, the office posts values after the first Monday in July, offers review through July 31, and says a formal protest must reach the chancery clerk by 9:00 a.m. on the first Monday in August.

Bring evidence about value. Lafayette County's appeal guide says boards weigh the fairness and accuracy of the value and that a recent appraisal of your own house is the best exhibit. Hinds has not published matching guidance we could confirm, but the same logic applies.

If an appraisal has the wrong square footage, the state says you may sometimes get a refund for prior years through the chancery clerk.

sections.h2: What happens if Hinds County taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
The house goes to the county tax sale on the last Monday in August, and if nobody bids, it is struck off to the state. The chancery clerk collects delinquent taxes, and once a year is delinquent the clerk says the older years must be cleared before the current year can be paid.

The clerk's page lists some firm rules for delinquent payments: no installments, and payment by cash or money order only, with no personal checks. The owner has two years from the sale date to redeem. If the two years pass, the property either matures to the state or the buyer receives a tax deed, which the clerk's own page describes as meaning you no longer own the property.

The state also publishes a Secretary of State line, 1-866-835-2637, for property that was sold to the state. Hinds posts delinquent and tax sale lists on its county site.

  • Redemption means paying the delinquent taxes plus statutory damages and interest, as Mississippi courts have described it.
  • An owner who sells before the sale date can clear the taxes from the sale proceeds.
  • An owner who waits until after the sale can still redeem, but only through the chancery clerk.

sections.h2: Selling a Hinds County house when property tax is still owed
sections.html:
You can sell a house with unpaid taxes, because taxes are cleared through the title and closing process. A title search turns up any back taxes, mortgages or other liens, and the balance is normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing.

The chancery clerk's guidance for buyers is useful for sellers too. A title search should be done before any money changes hands, and any attorney or title company can do it. The clerk's office itself may not search the records or prepare a deed. A deed must carry the seller's notarized signature, a legal description with indexing instructions, and the names, addresses and phone numbers of the sellers, buyers and preparer.

Timing matters if the house is occupied by an owner. The clerk notes that a buyer who occupies the home before January 1 can apply for homestead exemption from January 1 to April 1, which lowers that year's tax. A cash sale to an investor generally does not change the sequence, because the recording and tax steps are the same. It mainly removes the wait for a buyer's lender.

Sellers in Hinds County often arrive with older homes, inherited houses or rentals. Probate and heirship questions go to the chancery court, which hears probate and land matters, and the clerk's office files those papers. If the owner has died, clearing title may need to happen before a deed can be signed.

sections.h2: What should Hinds County sellers know about the local market around them?
sections.html:
Hinds County's economy leans on government, health care and education centered in Jackson. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Hinds County employment of 109,600 in December 2024, the highest of any Mississippi county. The University of Mississippi Medical Center, based in Jackson, says it has more than 10,000 full- and part-time employees.

Public schools are served by three districts: Jackson Public School District, Clinton Public School District and Hinds County School District. State-run schools for the blind and the deaf are also in the county. Colleges include Jackson State University, Millsaps College, Belhaven University, Mississippi College in Clinton and Hinds Community College in Raymond.

Population has been falling. The Census Bureau counted 250,998 people in 1980 and 227,742 in 2020, and estimates 211,888 for 2025. For a seller, that trend can mean fewer buyers per listing, and a clean tax record removes one obstacle to closing.

faqs.q: When are Hinds County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxes are due on or before February 1 for the previous assessment year. If that date falls on a weekend or legal holiday, you have until the next Monday without penalty or interest. After that, interest of one-half of one percent per month applies.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in Hinds County?
faqs.a: You pay the Hinds County Tax Collector, which has offices at 316 S. President St. in Jackson and 127 W. Main St. in Raymond. The office accepts cash, check or credit card with a 2.25 percent surcharge, and tags paid by personal check are held for 10 working days.

faqs.q: What is the Hinds County assessment ratio for a home?
faqs.a: An owner-occupied single-family home is assessed at 10 percent of true value, and other real property such as a rental is assessed at 15 percent. The assessed value is then multiplied by the combined millage rate of the county, city and school district.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Hinds County property assessment?
faqs.a: Normally the first Monday in August before the tax is due. You request a hearing with the Board of Supervisors through the Chancery Clerk, so start with the assessor well before that date.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Hinds County house if I owe back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company pays the back taxes from your proceeds at closing. If the house has already gone to tax sale, the chancery clerk collects the redemption amount, and the owner has two years from the sale date to redeem.
